analysis.one_liner: Requires 401(k) plan providers to disclose their fees and financial ties to workers and employers.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate health and labor committee in December 2007 and never received a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the nation's private pension law (ERISA) so that anyone selling services to a 401(k)-type plan had to tell the employer, in writing, exactly what services they provide, what they charge each year, and any side payments or financial relationships they have with other parties. Workers would have gotten a plain-English comparison chart of fees and investment options before choosing where their money goes, plus more detailed quarterly statements. The Labor Department would have surveyed fee levels, audited plans for compliance, and helped small employers pick affordable options [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly tens of millions of workers who save in 401(k)-style plans, whose retirement accounts are quietly reduced every year by fees they often cannot see or compare; small employers who sponsor plans but lack staff to untangle provider pricing would also get government help.

how_it_helps.text: Before a plan signs any service contract costing $5,000 or more per year (or 0.01% of plan assets), the provider must deliver a written statement itemizing investment management, recordkeeping, sales/commission, and other charges, and disclosing payments received from unaffiliated parties and free-or-discounted service arrangements [S3].

Workers must receive a notice at least 15 days before their first investment and before material changes, including a comparison chart of potential fees in four standard categories and a warning that options should be judged on fees, risk, and returns [S3].

Quarterly benefit statements would have to show the participant's balance, contributions, actual or estimated fees in dollars or expense ratio, asset allocation, and how their funds performed against a recognized market index [S3].

The Labor Department would annually publish survey data on plan fees, audit a representative sample of plans, publicly identify service providers whose practices block compliance, and provide small employers with educational and compliance materials [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Financial firms that sell recordkeeping, administration, and investment services to workplace retirement plans would bear the cost of itemized disclosure and would lose pricing power that comes from workers not seeing fees; employers would face new paperwork, though small plans get model forms and help [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Retirement plan service providers and employers

drawbacks.text: The bill relies entirely on disclosure: it caps no fees and bans no products, so a participant who ignores the charts still pays whatever the provider charges [S3].
Providers may satisfy much of the requirement with 'reasonable and representative estimates' rather than exact figures, which can leave workers with imprecise numbers [S3].

Plan administrators and employers, especially small ones, would face new paperwork duties, though the bill allows a small-plan exception and electronic delivery and directs the Secretary to offer compliance help [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off favors savers: 401(k) fees, even fractions of a percent a year, compound into large losses over a career, and the bill's main cost is paperwork and price transparency for providers. Its weakness is that disclosure alone depends on workers reading and acting on the charts. In the years after this bill died, the Labor Department went on to issue its own fee-disclosure rules, so workers eventually got much of this information without new legislation.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate committee it was referred to and died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Harkin introduced the bill on December 13, 2007, with Senator Herb Kohl as its only cosponsor [S3] [S4] [S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day [S5].
No further action was ever taken on the bill; it never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the 110th Congress ended [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Providers of 401(k) recordkeeping, administration, and investment services were better off, because fee structures and side payments stayed out of view rather than being forced into itemized written disclosure.

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and had introductory remarks printed in the record.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Edward Kennedy, D-IA predecessor chamber seat)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no action on it; no markup or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and its single cosponsor were Democrats, and the bill never reached a vote, so the partisan split was never tested.

industries.note: These firms charge fees deducted directly from workers' accounts, and the bill would have required them to itemize every component charge and disclose side payments before contracts are signed. Disclosure erodes the information advantage that lets fees stay high.

The bill targeted payments managers receive for being placed on a plan's investment menu, required disclosure of proprietary product use and share-class price differences, and would have mandated benchmark comparisons in participant notices. All of this exposes arrangements that generate revenue without appearing as a line-item fee.
Church and nonprofit school employees' 403(b) annuity contracts were brought under the same disclosure rules, threatening the opaque fee structures long common in that market.

They would face new compliance paperwork, but the bill directed the Labor Department to give them educational materials and help finding affordable investment options, and allowed small plans annual instead of quarterly statements.
